detail.longDescription: I'm adding terminal colours to one of my Python scripts. Initially I used global constants: def supports_color() -> bool: """Check whether terminal supports color""" ... return True if supports_color(): RED = "\033[31m" GREEN = "\033[32m" YELLOW = "\033[33m" BLUE = "\033[34m" PURPLE = "\033[0;35m" RESET = "\033[0m" else: RED = GREEN = YELLOW = BLUE = PURPLE = RESET = '' Then I attempted using a StrEnum : from enum import StrEnum class Color(StrEnum): if supports_color(): RED = "\033[31m" GREEN = "\033[32m" YELLOW = "\033[33m" BLUE = "\033[34m" PURPLE = "\033[0;35m" RESET = "\033[0m" else: RED = GREEN = YELLOW = BLUE = PURPLE = RESET = '' But Pyright flagged the assignments in the else clause, saying: Enum member "RED" is already declared Enum member "GREEN" is already declared ... Enum member "RESET" is already declared I tried breaking it down into multiple assignments, but the flag persisted: else: RED = '' GREEN = '' YELLOW = '' BLUE = '' PURPLE = '' RESET = '' However, the following works: s = supports_color() class Color(StrEnum): RED = "\033[31m" if s else '' GREEN = "\033[32m" if s else '' YELLOW = "\033[33m" if s else '' BLUE = "\033[34m" if s else '' PURPLE = "\033[0;35m" if s else '' RESET = "\033[0m" if s else '' Why does Pyright flag my first attempt, but not the others?
